Authoring bindings and exact content availability ### 16.1 Local names An authoring environment may supply a finite map from names to final BlueIds. A name is local syntax, not a type identity. Automatic substitution applies only at the type positions specified in §9. Ordinary text, `name`, and `description` are not rewritten because their values resemble an alias. A package mount assigns a prefix to selected exports. Mounting package X does not mount the aliases used by X's author or by X's dependency packages. To use dependency Y by name, the consumer MUST establish its own binding, for example `xyz/Order`. Definitions already published by X retain their exact references to Y, regardless of the consumer's bindings. **LANG-BINDING-SCOPE.** Binding addition MUST reject a name that is already bound to a different identity, without partially changing the environment. Repeating the same name-to-identity binding is permitted. Core aliases MUST NOT be rebound to different identities. Removing a mount removes its names and contributed provider layer; it does not revoke or delete separately retained immutable content. A mount prefix is a local name, not an instruction to execute code or fetch a URL. Prefix syntax for the package model is defined in §18. Independent applications may use different prefixes for identical definitions and obtain identical exact results. ### 16.2 Finalized cyclic-member aliases Alias targets may be plain final BlueIds or finalized cyclic-member IDs. A symbolic `this#i` is not a final alias target. Access to a finalized member requires its owning-set proof when the selected operation needs the member's body. A loader MUST preserve the member identity and MUST NOT replace it with the ordinary hash of the detached body. ### 16.3 Supporting content without additional names A content environment may contain definitions that have no authoring alias. A self-contained package may supply the exact definitions required by its exports without exposing the names of every supporting definition. Availability, naming, and execution support remain separate. Every supplied definition has the same identity, specialization, schema, collection-context, and admission rules as a definition supplied individually. Package membership creates neither an additional type kind nor an exemption from validation. Missing required content remains incomplete. ### 16.4 Reuse of established results Within an operation, verified immutable exact content and completed semantic obligations may be reused under keys that include the exact input, selected rules, recipe, goal, and root context. Active plans and unfinished obligations MUST NOT be cached as successful results. Reusing content across environments is permitted only under the evidence conditions of §5. Reusing a semantic result requires the same relevant interpretation. An ordinary-value cycle can establish structural presence as defined by the algorithms; a cycle of type edges cannot manufacture a concrete value. --- ## 17. Specification metadata ### 17.1 Meaning and shape `specification` is an OPTIONAL reserved metadata field alongside `name` and `description`. It identifies normative semantic context associated with the exact node. Unlike the two literal labels, its value is a node reference. In Source, the field accepts an explicit reference or an inline node. An inline target is prepared in its own context, retained as exact content, and replaced by its reference. Bare text is not a specification reference. To supply normative text inline, use an explicit Text node. Exact input may materialize the target; Direct input requires its pure reference. Symbolic local references are permitted only within the cyclic-set procedures in §12. ```yaml name: Example declaration description: A reusable declaration. specification: type: Text value: The additional rules governing this declaration. ``` This example defines the shape of the metadata; it does not establish a particular processor protocol. A plain field named `spec` is ordinary content and has no reserved metadata meaning. ### 17.2 Identity and payload structure **LANG-SPECIFICATION-IDENTITY.** The target's exact identity contributes to the containing node's identity as specified by the ordinary child-reference helper. Changing the target changes that contribution. An exact reference and a verified materialization of its target are interchangeable for identity. The metadata is permitted on object, scalar, list, and payload-free nodes. It does not create an object payload, establish value presence, or count toward ordinary field constraints. It is excluded from the ordinary business-field collection of an effective view. Resolution does not expand or merge the target's contents into the containing node. ### 17.3 Inheritance and refinement **LANG-SPECIFICATION-INHERITANCE.** A type's root specification is not copied into an instance as the instance's own metadata or as an ordinary field. Its association remains available through the exact type relation. A subtype may declare its own specification without deleting the base type's association. For a type A associated with SA, a subtype B associated with SB, and an instance x whose type is B and which has no own specification: | Observation | Result | |---|---| | x's own specification | Absent | | B's own specification | SB | | A's own specification | SA | | Declared associations along x's type chain | SB followed by SA | A specification association does not override the underlying type's content guarantees. If a concrete inherited child already has fixed metadata, an explicit refinement cannot substitute conflicting metadata. The comparison is atomic: it is not a recursive merge of two normative documents. ### 17.4 Observations and required evidence `query` of `/specification` or a root `specification` observation reports the node's own reference or Absent. Traversal below that metadata explicitly requests the referenced content. The processor must obtain the necessary verified evidence to answer such a traversal. Structural identity can use a final reference without its body. Strict admission verifies reachable content, declared types, and the specification target in the definition role. A missing target is incomplete evidence; a body with a mismatching identity is invalid evidence. A reference to reusable normative structure is not required to satisfy every completed business-value obligation merely because it appears as metadata. **LANG-SPECIFICATION-ROLE.** Definition-valid target content is not proof that the target is a complete protocol descriptor, that its prose is consistent, or that a processor implements it. Those conclusions require their own role-specific checks. ### 17.5 Discovery through a type chain The following procedure defines the direct type-chain association observation. It does not recursively activate every specification in an arbitrary content graph and does not resolve semantic prerequisites beyond that chain. ```python """Read governing metadata along a selected type chain; not a support assertion. Does not activate protocols, execute code, or scan unrelated provider records. """ from algorithms import blue as B def declared_requirements(node, context): result=[]; seen=set(); current=node while current is not None: identity=B.identity(current) B.require(identity not in seen, 'TypeCycle', identity) seen.add(identity) body=B.open_exact(current,context) link=body.get(B.SPECIFICATION) if link is not B.ABSENT: B.require(isinstance(link,B.Ref), 'InvalidNodeShape', 'specification position') result.append({'definedOn':identity,'specification':link.id}) parent=body.get('type') current=parent if isinstance(parent,B.Ref) and parent.id not in B.CORE_NAME else None return tuple(result) ``` The result identifies both the definition declaring the association and the target specification identity. Identical target specifications on different declaring types may appear more than once. Type cycles remain invalid according to §6. ### 17.6 Normative rules versus informative documentation A governing specification establishes additional semantic obligations. A guide explains use without introducing such obligations. A package may contain guides, examples, and specialized programs without defining a new protocol. A program fully expressed using existing primitives need not declare a new native protocol merely because it is published independently. Its existing type and primitive associations remain applicable in their defined roles. Conversely, an unrecognized executable declaration does not become interpretable merely by omitting specification metadata. --- ## 18. Standard packages and protocol descriptors ### 18.1 Package model A **package** is an immutable Blue document that identifies a selected collection of exports, exact imports, specifications, and documentation. A **source repository** is an authoring workspace; it is not itself the package identity. A **bundle** is an explicit selection of package mounts. A **registry** is a retrieval or discovery service. Package and Protocol Specification are ordinary standard definitions. Their complete Source definitions are included in Appendix C. Their identities are calculated using ordinary admission and identity operations. No core primitive, reserved `Package` keyword, or alternative hash function is introduced by those definitions. A package processor applies the role checks in this section in addition to Language checks. Package roots are admitted in the definition role because their graphs contain reusable definitions. The package-role checks then establish complete package structure, export validity, and supplied evidence. A tool MUST NOT reinterpret failed value admission as successful package admission without selecting the package role explicitly. ### 18.2 Semantic root and witness This edition uses the package model identifier `blue-package-model/2-specification-metadata`. The identifier is an exact format label, not a compatibility range. The root has the following fields. A semantic witness is the complete authoring-shaped record used to reproduce and verify the exact root; null optional witness slots are omitted by normal Source preparation. | Field | Required meaning | |---|---| | `type` | Exact reference to the ordinary Package definition in Appendix C. | | `format` | The exact package model identifier above. | | `name` | The package's identifying literal name. It is not a globally unique authority or a registry locator. | | `version` | A human-facing release label. It does not perform dependency resolution or establish compatibility. | | `identityProfile` | The exact supported Language algorithm profile selected before admission. For this edition: `blue-language/2026-09-26-specification-metadata-1`. | | `bootstrapLanguage` | Boolean indicating a bootstrap Language release. | | `language` | Reference to the exact selected bootstrap Language package, or null in the bootstrap witness. | | `exports` | Map from local export names to exact definition references. | | `imports` | Map from explicit local prefixes to exact imported package references. | | `protocol` | Reference to this package's governing protocol descriptor, or null when it defines no new protocol. | | `specBindings` | Verified associations from exported type identities to native specification references and the selected descriptor. | | `declaredRequirements` | List of exact protocol-descriptor references required by the package's declared use. | | `documentation` | Map from safe logical paths to identified Text assets and their byte descriptors. | Semantic witness keys are exactly those listed. Additional distribution metadata belongs outside the semantic root. The exact Blue document is the normal admitted result of this record, not its raw JSON byte hash. The release-label grammar is `major.minor.patch`, with nonnegative decimal components having no leading zeros except zero itself, and an optional hyphen followed by dot-separated alphanumeric/hyphen prerelease identifiers. Numeric prerelease identifiers have no redundant leading zeros. The label is descriptive; comparisons of labels MUST NOT substitute one identity for another. ### 18.3 Language bootstrap A bootstrap Language package has `bootstrapLanguage: true`, no `language` reference, no imports, and no protocol descriptor. Its rule selection comes from the implementation establishing that bootstrap context. It may export ordinary standard definitions and carry this complete specification as documentation. A non-bootstrap package has `bootstrapLanguage: false`, an exact Language reference, and an explicit direct import of that same Language package. Every semantically interpreted imported package must have the same Language selection. An imported bootstrap must be that exact selected package. These checks also apply to transitive dependencies and previously visited dependencies; a foreign bootstrap cannot bypass the check by being reached through another branch. This is the supported interpretation of this edition, not an assertion that every possible later Language edition must have identical representation or algorithms. §19 defines the versioning boundary. The bootstrap Package and Protocol Specification nodes need not point back to their containing Language package. Their standard role is established by the selected Language. Publishing them does not impose a package-to-type-to-package cycle. ### 18.4 Exports and scoped imports An export name is a nonempty string associated with one final BlueId. Exported targets MUST be available as verifiable exact definitions, including required cyclic proofs. There is no automatic historical-to-current identity substitution. An import binds one exact package to an explicit prefix within the importing author's source environment. For this package model a prefix matches: ```text @?[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*(/[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*)* ``` For example, `orders`, `company/workflows`, and `@repo.blue` are permitted. A consumer constructs a local name by appending `/` and a selected export name. The resulting binding is a normal Language alias, subject to collision checks and the reserved core bindings. **LANG-PACKAGE-SCOPE.** Importing X does not introduce the aliases that X used for its imports. If X refers to Y1, mounting Y2 directly does not retarget that reference. A consumer may mount multiple exact package versions under distinct prefixes. Such coexistence does not establish that their types are interchangeable or that all associated protocols can be combined. Package import graphs MUST be acyclic in this model. Cyclic definitions within packages use §12; they are not cyclic package imports. Multiple paths to the same exact package are permitted and MUST be verified consistently. Retrieval locations, package version labels, and mount order do not select a different target. ### 18.5 Supporting exact content Supporting records provide the exact definitions and evidence required to establish exports and identified package content. They do not automatically add aliases, authorize actions, or install processor code. A selected package can therefore make an unnamed referenced Order definition available without mounting any `Orders/Order` alias. A self-contained package supplies the required exact content and owning-set proofs. A partial content delivery MAY be retained as partial evidence, but MUST NOT be represented as a successfully verified self-contained package. A receiver MUST distinguish a missing body from a known absent field. A package's own exported definitions and supplied supporting definitions retain their exact identities independently of which package distributes them. A package that re-exports a definition MUST NOT modify its description or metadata while asserting that the original identity is preserved. ### 18.6 Protocol Specification role A protocol descriptor uses the ordinary Protocol Specification type. Its required fields are `type`, `name`, `language`, `rules`, `requires`, and `status`. Its optional fields are `effectiveRules` and `schedulingPolicy`. This is a descriptor schema, not an instruction to execute new behavior. | Field | Meaning | |---|---| | `type` | Exact reference to the Protocol Specification definition in Appendix C. | | `name` | Literal protocol name; not a dispatch or authority key. | | `language` | The same selected Language reference as the package context. | | `rules` | Exact reference to accessible Text containing the governing normative material. | | `requires` | Map from local requirement labels to exact protocol-descriptor references. Labels are local explanatory names. | | `status` | Publisher's Text classification of the descriptor. It is not certification or a trust grant. | | `effectiveRules` | Optional exact Text reference to an explicitly identified complete statement or supplement. | | `schedulingPolicy` | Optional exact Text reference to an explicitly selected policy. The field's existence does not make scheduling a Language operation. | A descriptor is admitted in the definition role, then checked for its complete descriptor structure. Its referenced rule documents MUST be established as Text. All protocol prerequisites use the same Language selection. The prerequisite graph MUST be acyclic. A descriptor cannot authorize an arbitrary replacement of its required protocol by a later release. Where supplementary rule documents are supplied, the protocol's normative content must define how they apply. The field names do not provide a generic override or precedence mechanism. A contradictory or incomplete prose contract is not repaired by a matching package hash. A package may define no new protocol. Specialized programs, clauses, schemas, or forms expressed through existing semantics may use informative documentation alone. An empty export set is permitted for an explicitly declared protocol package; the package need not invent operator types solely to distribute a specification. ### 18.7 Native specification associations In this package profile, a protocol package associates each of its own exports with its governing rules using native `specification` metadata. Its `specBindings` map is keyed by each exported definition identity and contains: ```json { "specification": {"blueId": "RULES_ID"}, "protocol": {"blueId": "DESCRIPTOR_ID"}, "binding": "native-metadata" } ``` The symbolic strings in this example stand for valid final identities. `RULES_ID` MUST equal the descriptor's `rules` target. The definition's own exact `specification` MUST contain that reference. `DESCRIPTOR_ID` MUST equal the package's selected protocol. Bindings cover exactly the package's exports when it has a protocol; otherwise the binding map is empty. Imported definitions retain their own associations in their imported package witnesses. A package does not acquire a new native implementation merely by copying these records. A bootstrap Language package is governed by its selected Language role rather than by a self-referential protocol descriptor. Changing the native rules reference changes the containing definition's identity. Adding a guide to the package without changing that reference does not change the definition. A package descriptor MUST NOT assign conflicting native semantics to an unchanged type through uncommitted explanatory metadata. ### 18.8 Declared requirements `declaredRequirements` is separate from `imports`. A library may import a protocol's data definitions without declaring that every consumer performs that protocol's task. A publisher selects direct imported protocol requirements explicitly; it may include the selected package's own protocol. Transitive prerequisites are followed through exact descriptor references. The package-level requirement list is an inventory for the declared use. It is not a proof of document-specific support, structural validity, or authorization. A processor still applies the relevant checks to actual content in the roles defined by its protocols. Omitting an execution requirement does not enable an unknown executable primitive. ### 18.9 Documentation and package identity Every included asset in this package profile is valid UTF-8 Text. A documentation entry contains exactly `content`, `sha256`, and `size`: ```json { "content": {"blueId": "TEXT_DOCUMENT_ID"}, "sha256": "sha256:HEX_DIGEST_OF_UTF8_BYTES", "size": 123 } ``` The Text value is encoded as UTF-8 to establish the byte digest and byte count. The package processor verifies the Text identity, byte descriptor, and delivered file contents. A source publisher in this profile uses LF line endings and no UTF-8 BOM; it must not silently normalize an already identified Text value. A logical path is relative, nonempty, uses `/` separators, and cannot address a parent, root, drive, or external location. Archive consumers also reject unsafe paths, duplicates, symbolic links, and file-type tricks before installation. Host-specific byte and extraction limits are operational safeguards, not alternative Language identity rules. The package BlueId commits to its exact semantic root and referenced definitions, imports, and documentation. It does not commit to registry hostname, cache path, archive compression, CI run, credential, or source-checkout path unless such text is deliberately included as declared content. The root's own computed identity is not inserted into that root before hashing. ### 18.10 Verification procedure **LANG-PACKAGE-VERIFY.** A package processor claiming a verified package MUST: 1. Establish the supported Language/profile and the expected package identity, when one is supplied, before semantic interpretation. 2. Parse the carrier without duplicate keys or unsafe file entries; verify its declared byte inventory. 3. Admit the exact package root in the definition role and require its recomputed BlueId to equal the requested package identity. 4. Verify each semantic package witness as the same ordinary admitted content it describes. Enforce the root field set, format, version shape, bootstrap rules, imports, and Language consistency. 5. Traverse package imports and protocol prerequisites with cycle detection. Revisited nodes do not bypass context checks. 6. Establish every selected rule document and the native specification associations. 7. Admit every export as a definition, preserving owning-set evidence for cyclic members. 8. Establish every documentation target as Text and verify its byte descriptor and, for files supplied by this artifact, exact file bytes. 9. Verify all supplied records and their agreement between indexes, package evidence, and exported-content evidence. Do not certify extra unrelated witnesses as part of the root's identified closure. 10. Return a verified package result only after those checks succeed. A partial or failed operation does not install a successful mount. This procedure does not certify that a protocol's requirements are implemented or that an author is trusted. Expected identity must be selected through the caller's own trusted context. Matching a checksum shipped beside an untrusted archive alone does not establish that it is the artifact the caller intended to obtain. ### 18.11 Reference archive profile The implemented archive profile is identified by the literal string `blue-package/0.3-local`. This historical format label identifies the byte carrier; it is not an instruction to use an earlier interpretation or a publication-status assertion. An equivalent implementation may use another transport while preserving the package-role requirements. The ZIP contains four structural files plus the identified Text assets: | File | Role | |---|---| | `package.blue.json` | Exact normalized package-root document. | | `package-records.json` | Exact provider records and owning-set evidence for the root's required content. | | `repository.json` | Explicit exported alias map and backing definition records. | | `package.json` | Distribution manifest containing file inventory, semantic witnesses, and provenance. | The distribution manifest records `packageBlueId`, `languageProfile`, `language`, `protocol`, exports, exact import pins, semantic package/specification witnesses, file byte descriptors, and validation information. These claims MUST agree with the identified root and verified records. Producer source hashes and URLs are provenance, not alternative semantic identities or proof of conformance. The repository carrier has `format`, `name`, `aliases`, `records`, `metadata`, and `identity`. Its format is `blue-python-repository/1`. Its `identity` is a SHA-256 checksum of the canonical envelope without that identity field, not a BlueId. The profile's precise envelope serialization and verification procedures are included in Appendix F. The same data can be consumed by implementations in languages other than Python. The semantic witness for an imported package is not a source program to be reparsed under a different registry. Reconstructing and admitting its declared root must produce its existing package BlueId. A registry's readable tag is only a lookup hint. Normal verification never upgrades an import, edits a lock, or rewrites an exported type. --- ## 19. Edition selection and cyclic identity boundaries ### 19.1 Scope of an edition A Language edition fixes the node model, input interpretation, registry, exact-identity procedures, type and schema semantics, and operation evidence rules. A document or package is interpreted under an established edition, not under the most recently available package with a matching name. The exact Language release is selected out of band before semantic processing. An envelope may identify a package and the required profile; the interpreter must verify those claims under a supported selection. Nested references do not select alternate interpreters independently. ### 19.2 Compatibility **LANG-EDITION-COMPATIBILITY.** This edition defines no general cross-edition conversion or semantic-import mechanism. Its package processor uses the exact Language selection required by §18. A release label, matching major version, equal-looking schema, or compatibility claim in untrusted package content does not relax that requirement. A later Language specification may define compatibility with an earlier one. Such a specification must state the operations covered, the preserved identities and observations, and how earlier evidence is verified. No machine-readable compatibility vocabulary, automatic version solver, or generic permission to mix editions is defined here. An implementation that merely stores or transfers a foreign artifact need not interpret it. Supporting two editions in separate contexts does not itself establish semantic composition between them. A processor that cannot establish the required interpretation reports unsupported processing; it does not recalculate old references under another edition or treat unavailable interpretation as a malformed original document. ### 19.3 Cyclic sets **LANG-CYCLE-EDITION.** A symbolic set, its preliminary ordering, master identity, canonical member mapping, final materializations, and owning-set proof MUST be constructed and verified under one selected Language interpretation. The algorithm cannot switch editions between members or between finalization and verification. External references in that set must be interpretable under the same established context. A foreign member body is not evidence of a current-edition member identity. A resolver MUST NOT hash an older detached body using a newer procedure and treat the result as verification of its former `MASTER#index` address. A specification that permits cross-edition composition must define the behavior of complete owning sets, external references, canonical ordering, and proof verification. Compatibility of acyclic scalar values alone is insufficient to establish that behavior. This edition grants no implicit compatibility for those cases. ### 19.4 Publication boundaries are not cyclic-identity boundaries Ordinary package imports and protocol prerequisite graphs are acyclic in this package model. A package may nevertheless contain definitions whose ordinary content references form finalized cyclic sets. These are different graphs and different checks. A cyclic member may be exported under several names or distributed in several artifacts. Its owning set and proof do not change merely because its publication location changes. An artifact claiming self-contained use must retain the required proof. The package or filename is not a substitute for that proof. ### 19.5 Revision and identity preservation A package-only documentation change may change the package BlueId while retaining unchanged type and specification identities. A change to exact type content changes the type identity. A changed governing-specification reference also changes any exact node that carries it. A dependency mount does not migrate previously published content. A processor MUST retain the edition and scope of validation evidence. A new Language selection does not retroactively validate old admission receipts, even when an exact node happens to retain the same BlueId. Migration is an explicitly established new operation, not a display conversion or a consequence of loading another package. --- ## 20. Protocol interpretation and document processors ### 20.1 Additional interpretations A **document processor** interprets Blue content to perform a defined task under a selected Language and applicable protocol specifications. A task may evaluate expressions, execute workflows, coordinate histories, render a form, evaluate a query, run a simulation, or verify a proof. No universal event-processing method or effect model is imposed by Language. A **protocol specification** identifies the additional rules and their exact prerequisites. It may govern several kinds of nodes and the relationships between them. It is not necessarily a predicate applied independently to each node. The standard Protocol Specification type and descriptor role are defined in §18. A Language implementation may store or inspect such content without implementing the protocol itself. ### 20.2 Support claims **LANG-PROCESSOR-SUPPORT.** A processor claiming to perform a protocol task MUST implement the exact required rules and the applicable prerequisites for that task. Availability of specification text, a matching package name, or a successfully verified type is not evidence of implementation support. Support declarations identify exact specifications and, where necessary, supported combinations and roles. A tool MUST NOT claim complete support while silently ignoring an applicable required interpretation. It MAY expose unsupported content as data without claiming the unsupported result. A provider or user-supplied package cannot install trusted runtime bindings by declaring that it is compatible. A support decision is made by the installed implementation and the selected context. This specification does not define a standard HTTP capability endpoint or an executable plugin installation protocol. ### 20.3 Applicability The selected protocol determines the roles and boundaries at which additional meaning applies. A processor MUST account for the relevant definitions, their inherited requirements, and declared semantic prerequisites in those roles. It MUST NOT globally activate all specifications mentioned in every mounted package, example, or supporting record. Package imports provide names and content. Declared protocol requirements provide semantic prerequisites. Neither alone proves that a particular document is valid or that a business operation is authorized. A document-specific support check is distinct from a package-level requirement inventory. Introducing a new required executable or managed structure requires support checking before that structure is interpreted or activated. A prior check of a different exact state is not evidence about arbitrary future content. ### 20.4 Structural extension boundary This edition reserves `contracts` as a structural attachment that may accompany scalar, list, or object payloads. Language parses, identifies, and refines it; Language does not execute it. An application protocol may assign interpretation to that content in a defined task. Other application names remain ordinary fields unless listed as reserved in this Language edition. A package cannot add a Language-reserved word, change payload classification, or change identity contribution by placing a declaration in its documentation. A different structural attachment mechanism requires a Language specification that defines it. ### 20.5 Examples of independent protocol roles — informative A rendering protocol can define a Form and Text Field, with their types identifying the rendering rules. An application package can specialize Text Field with a fixed label without creating a new rendering protocol. A generic Language reader can inspect the resulting form; a rendering processor is required to produce the specified interaction. A query protocol can define filters, projections, and their evaluation rules. A library of queries using those primitives supplies programs rather than a new evaluator. A scientific-transformation package can likewise supply computations, units, or input constraints through an existing expression protocol. A workflow protocol can define step order and effects. A coordination protocol can add source evidence, authority, and history rules. A package of commercial workflows may use those rules without requiring an implementation for every exported commercial type. A newly defined native scheduling rule, however, is additional behavior that an implementation must support explicitly. ### 20.6 Authority and consistency A protocol dependency does not authorize redefinition of the required protocol. Two incompatible rules cannot be combined merely by importing both packages. The selected task must have an explicitly defined, coherent interpretation; import order is not a conflict-resolution procedure. No Language operation proves arbitrary prose specifications mutually consistent. It establishes exact content and the checks within its defined role. Conformance, domain validation, authenticity, and authorization remain distinct claims. ## Appendix A. Algorithm notation and primitive operations The code in Appendix D is normative executable notation. `Node` is an immutable set of uniquely named exact contributions; `Ref` is a final content reference; `Local` is a temporary cyclic-set edge. `ABSENT` is a distinguished sentinel, not JSON null. Lists and tuples are ordered. Maps have unique string keys. Sets are used for membership and logical conjunction; their physical iteration order does not establish a different portable content result. `int` denotes an arbitrary-precision mathematical integer, distinct from Boolean. `Fraction` denotes an exact reduced rational with positive denominator. `float` denotes a finite IEEE 754 binary64 value where admitted. `struct` bit conversions use the indicated fixed byte order. `Decimal` is used only to construct or inspect exact decimal candidates as specified; it does not authorize rounding where exact rational comparison is required. Integer division, remainder, greatest common divisor, bit shifts, and bit length have their usual exact mathematical meanings. Strings are sequences of Unicode scalar values. Strict UTF-8 decoding rejects malformed encodings and unpaired surrogate content. `key_order` encodes UTF-16 code units solely to determine the required object-key order. JSON `\\u` escapes decode to scalar values; decoded keys, not their source spelling, determine duplicates. Required JSON escapes are quotation mark, reverse solidus, and control characters U+0000–U+001F; the canonical encoder uses the specified short escapes and lowercase four-digit hexadecimal escapes for the remaining controls. Input JSON uses objects, arrays, strings, decimal number tokens, `true`, `false`, and `null`. Object names are strings. Insignificant whitespace consists of space, tab, carriage return, and line feed. There is exactly one root value and no trailing non-whitespace. A number uses the complete grammar in §3.1. The decoder must preserve number-token spelling until the Blue scalar codec selects its category. Comments, trailing commas, hexadecimal numbers, NaN, and Infinity are not JSON tokens. Portable YAML is a presentation of the same mappings, sequences, and scalars. Its indentation, flow collections, quoted strings, block folding, and chomping produce a syntax tree; the Blue scalar resolver in §3 is applied rather than a schema-dependent native YAML resolver. Anchors, aliases, tags, directives, implicit timestamps, merge keys, and multiple documents are excluded. The reference parser in Appendix D rejects those constructs before node normalization. Parser implementation choice does not authorize accepting additional Blue scalar types. `hashlib.sha256` denotes SHA-256 of exactly the supplied byte string, producing 32 digest bytes; it is not a generic selectable hash. Padding is a one bit, zeros to leave 64 bits in the final 512-bit block, and the original bit length in big-endian form. The 64 rounds use 32-bit words, addition modulo 2^32, the SHA-256 choice/majority functions, and its fixed initial values and constants. Blue then applies its independently specified base58 encoding, not hex encoding or a multihash wrapper. `copy` operations preserve values; object identity is not content. `lru_cache` and context memoization are optimizations whose reuse must obey §§5 and 16. `dataclass` and `typing` describe records, not additional wire fields. Exceptions carry the defined semantic outcomes; an equivalent implementation may use tagged return values. The only non-Blue syntax composition supplied by a library in the executable notation is the permitted JSON/YAML parser. All Blue-specific scalar resolution, canonical formatting, identity, structural validation, schema processing, graph access, and cyclic-set decisions are included below. A host's default serializer or numeric coercion is not a replacement for these procedures. ### A.1 SHA-256 compression definition The eight initial words, written in hexadecimal, are: ```text 6a09e667 bb67ae85 3c6ef372 a54ff53a 510e527f 9b05688c 1f83d9ab 5be0cd19 ``` The sixty-four round constants are: ```text 428a2f98 71374491 b5c0fbcf e9b5dba5 3956c25b 59f111f1 923f82a4 ab1c5ed5 d807aa98 12835b01 243185be 550c7dc3 72be5d74 80deb1fe 9bdc06a7 c19bf174 e49b69c1 efbe4786 0fc19dc6 240ca1cc 2de92c6f 4a7484aa 5cb0a9dc 76f988da 983e5152 a831c66d b00327c8 bf597fc7 c6e00bf3 d5a79147 06ca6351 14292967 27b70a85 2e1b2138 4d2c6dfc 53380d13 650a7354 766a0abb 81c2c92e 92722c85 a2bfe8a1 a81a664b c24b8b70 c76c51a3 d192e819 d6990624 f40e3585 106aa070 19a4c116 1e376c08 2748774c 34b0bcb5 391c0cb3 4ed8aa4a 5b9cca4f 682e6ff3 748f82ee 78a5636f 84c87814 8cc70208 90befffa a4506ceb bef9a3f7 c67178f2 ``` For each padded block, let W[0..15] be its big-endian 32-bit words. For t from 16 to 63: ```text small0(x) = ROTR(x,7) XOR ROTR(x,18) XOR (x >> 3) small1(x) = ROTR(x,17) XOR ROTR(x,19) XOR (x >> 10) W[t] = small1(W[t-2]) + W[t-7] + small0(W[t-15]) + W[t-16] ``` Initialize a..h from the current eight hash words. Each round t performs: ```text big0(x) = ROTR(x,2) XOR ROTR(x,13) XOR ROTR(x,22) big1(x) = ROTR(x,6) XOR ROTR(x,11) XOR ROTR(x,25) Ch(x,y,z) = (x AND y) XOR ((NOT x) AND z) Maj(x,y,z) = (x AND y) XOR (x AND z) XOR (y AND z) T1 = h + big1(e) + Ch(e,f,g) + K[t] + W[t] T2 = big0(a) + Maj(a,b,c) (h,g,f,e,d,c,b,a) = (g,f,e,d+T1,c,b,a,T1+T2) ``` All additions and complements are 32-bit. Add the final a..h to the current hash words modulo 2^32. Concatenate the final words in big-endian order to obtain the digest. For the empty byte string, its hexadecimal rendering is `e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855`. ## Appendix B. ## Appendix F. Exact repository carrier This appendix fixes the integrity and evidence rules of the `blue-python-repository/1` carrier used by §18.11. It is an interoperable data carrier, not a requirement to use Python and not a separate Blue identity scheme. Its envelope checksum is the lowercase hexadecimal SHA-256 of UTF-8 JSON with keys ordered as Unicode scalar strings, no optional whitespace, unescaped non-ASCII scalar characters, and no nonfinite numeric values, after omitting the `identity` field. The checksum is prefixed by `sha256:`. This envelope encoding must not be substituted for the Language helper encoding when calculating a BlueId. The envelope contains exactly `format`, `name`, `aliases`, `records`, `metadata`, and `identity`. `name` is a nonempty package/repository label. `aliases` maps strings to valid final identities; core names cannot be rebound. `records` maps final identities to declared exact bodies or owning-set proofs. A non-core alias needs its target record. A record cannot be accepted merely because its key has a valid identifier spelling. Each record is independently opened under the selected Language and verified against its key. A Text record has `mode: "exact"`, `format: "json"` or `"yaml"`, and `text` containing the original body. A cyclic record contains the complete `proof` and may include a separately supplied `body`; its verification follows §12. Inline and referenced bodies use the same evidence rules. Metadata is non-authoritative carrier information unless separately committed by the package root. It must not install aliases or imply executable support. Structural carrier verification is distinct from `audit`, which admits every exported target as a definition. A package processor also verifies the ordinary Package root, its documentary assets, semantic witnesses, and reachable-record agreement. No carrier checksum or audit count replaces those steps. Implementations can transmit equivalent verified content using a different physical record carrier. A consumer that claims this particular envelope format must follow its exact checksum, required-key, alias, and record-verification rules. "}
